Burns: Immediate First-Aid Care
Health Awareness Reference — General Public Guidance
Burns can result from heat, hot liquids, flames, electricity, chemicals, or friction, and range from minor to life-threatening. Prompt, correct first aid — especially early cooling of the burn — reduces pain, limits tissue damage, and improves healing. This reference is intended for general public awareness and quick recall in an emergency.
What to Do Immediately
Stop the burning process first. Move the person away from the heat source, flames, electrical current, or chemical to prevent further injury. Turn off the electrical source before touching someone injured by electricity.
Smother flames if present. If clothing is on fire, have the person stop, drop to the ground, and roll to smother the flames, or smother the flames with a blanket or cloth.
Remove restrictive items near the burn area. Take off jewellery, watches, belts, and tight clothing near the burn before swelling begins. If clothing is stuck to the burnt skin, do not pull it off — leave it in place.
Cool the burn with cool running water. Hold the burnt area under cool (not ice-cold) running water for about 20 minutes, as soon as possible after the injury. If running water isn't available, use a clean, cool, wet cloth, changing it regularly.
Cover the burn loosely. After cooling, cover the burn loosely with a clean, non-fluffy cloth or sterile non-stick dressing to protect it from air and contamination. Do not wrap tightly.
Check for and remove constricting items on burnt limbs. If fingers or toes are burnt, or jewellery is on a swelling limb, remove rings, bangles, and similar items as soon as possible before swelling increases.
Keep the person warm elsewhere on the body. Keep the person warm with a blanket over unaffected areas of the body, while keeping the burnt area cool, to help prevent the person from becoming too cold.
Offer simple pain relief if appropriate. Give paracetamol at the standard recommended dose if available and the person can swallow safely, to help ease discomfort while awaiting further care.
Seek professional medical care for anything beyond a minor burn. For large, deep, or high-risk burns, or if you are unsure of severity, call emergency medical services right away and continue cooling while waiting for help.
What NOT to Do
Do not apply ice or ice-cold water to a burn. Ice or freezing-cold water can reduce blood flow to the burn, worsen tissue damage, and even cause hypothermia in larger burns; use cool running water instead.
Do not apply butter, oil, toothpaste, ghee, or other home remedies to a burn. These home remedies can trap heat, introduce infection, and make medical assessment more difficult; they are not supported by current burn-care evidence.
Do not burst or pick at blisters. Breaking a blister increases the risk of infection and slows healing; leave blisters intact and let a healthcare provider manage them if needed.
Do not pull off clothing that is stuck to the burnt skin. Clothing that has stuck to a burn can tear the skin if forced off; leave it in place and let medical staff manage it.
Do not use fluffy cotton wool or adhesive bandages directly on a burn. Cotton wool and fluffy dressings can shed fibres into the wound and stick to the burn; use a clean, non-fluffy cloth or proper sterile dressing instead.
Do not wrap the burn tightly. Tight wrapping can restrict blood flow, especially as the area swells; cover the burn loosely instead.
Do not rely on raw potato, aloe vera gel, or other unverified traditional remedies as primary treatment. The value of these treatments is unproven and they can delay proper cooling and professional care; stick to cool running water and a clean covering.
Do not assume all burns can be managed at home. Even minor-looking burns on the face, hands, feet, joints, or genitals, and all chemical, electrical, or large burns, need medical assessment.
When to Call Emergency Services
Call emergency medical services immediately (and do not wait to see if the situation improves) if any of the following apply:
The burn is large (larger than the person's palm) or covers more than one body part.
The burn is deep, with white, leathery, charred, or blackened skin.
The burn involves the face, hands, feet, joints, genitals, or airway (including singed nasal hair, cough, or difficulty breathing after smoke exposure).
The burn was caused by electricity or chemicals.
There is a lot of swelling, or the person shows signs of shock — pale, clammy skin, rapid breathing, weakness, or confusion.
The person is a young child, an elderly person, pregnant, or has other health conditions that increase risk.
The burn shows signs of infection later — increasing pain, redness, swelling, pus, or fever.
You are unsure how serious the burn is — when in doubt, it is always safer to seek medical care.
Minor burns (small, superficial, with intact skin) can often be cared for at home after cooling and covering, but should still be watched closely for worsening pain, spreading redness, or signs of infection over the following days.
Source Basis
This document is based on general, publicly available first-aid guidance for burns from established health and emergency-medicine organizations, paraphrased in original wording for awareness purposes. It does not quote any source directly.
World Health Organization (WHO) — burns first aid guidance
Australian and New Zealand Committee on Resuscitation (ANZCOR) — Guideline 9.1.3, First Aid for Burns
American Burn Association — Burn First Aid guidance
International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) — First Aid Task Force evidence review on burn cooling
General public emergency-medicine and first-aid training resources
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
